substantive_math_issues.subject: quotient by reducible polynomial need not be a field
substantive_math_issues.finding: The source queue's context describes F[x]/(f) as a field K for a merely nonconstant polynomial f. This is false if f is reducible (e.g. f=x² over Q): F[x]/(f) is a ring with nilpotents. The residue class of x is a root in that quotient ring, but to claim an extension field of the specific quotient one must require f irreducible. This is a genuine source-context qualification; do not silently alter effective occurrences.
substantive_math_issues.suggested_edit: If f is nonconstant irreducible, let K=F[x]/(f); then the class of x is a root of f in K. If f is arbitrary nonconstant, state only that xbar is a root in the quotient F-algebra F[x]/(f), which may fail to be a field.

items.original_mathematical_context: Set theory: binary intersection A∩U of two sets, whose elements belong to both A and U; applied to ambient open sets and a subspace.
items.mathematical_definition_draft: For sets A and U, their intersection is A∩U={x:x∈A and x∈U}.
typed_assumptions_and_edge_cases: Intersection is commutative, associative and idempotent.
A∩∅=∅; A∩X=A whenever A⊆X.
For a topological subspace A⊆X, A∩U is open in A when U is open in X; the subspace-topology conclusion is additional.

items.original_mathematical_context: Set theory: relative complement A\B={x∈A:x∉B} for two sets A,B⊆X; in the sigma-algebra axiom A,B are members of Σ.
items.mathematical_definition_draft: For sets A,B, the difference A\B is {x∈A:x∉B}. If A,B⊆X, it equals A∩(X\B).
typed_assumptions_and_edge_cases: A\B depends on the order of A and B.
A\A=∅, A\∅=A and ∅\B=∅.
Membership in a σ-algebra is a condition on A,B, not part of the set difference operation.

items.original_query: commutative unital algebra over a field
items.original_mathematical_context: Commutative algebra: commutative unital algebra A over a specified base field k, with a chosen unital structure homomorphism k→A; A need not be a field, a domain or geometrically regular.
items.term: Commutative unital algebra over a field
items.mathematical_definition_draft: Given a field k, a commutative unital k-algebra is a commutative unital ring A equipped with a specified unital ring homomorphism ι:k→A; equivalently it is a k-vector space with associative commutative k-bilinear multiplication having an identity 1_A and compatible scalar action.
typed_assumptions_and_edge_cases: If A≠0 then ι is injective because its kernel is an ideal of a field and ι(1)=1_A≠0.
If zero rings are admitted, A=0 is an algebra under the unital-map convention with 1_A=0; do not silently assume injectivity for this case.
No assumption of integrality, finite dimension, geometric reducedness or being a field.

items.original_mathematical_context: Commutative algebra: principal ideal generated by one element
items.term: Principal ideal generated by one element
items.mathematical_definition_draft: For an element a of a commutative unital ring R, the principal ideal (a) is aR={ra:r∈R}. It is the smallest ideal of R containing a.
typed_assumptions_and_edge_cases: (0) is the zero ideal; (1)=R, and (u)=R for any unit u.
In a noncommutative ring, left, right and two-sided generated ideals need separate definitions; the present context is commutative.
Being principal is an ideal's generation property, not a statement that its generator is prime.

items.original_mathematical_context: Set theory: bijective mapping f:X→Y, a function that is both injective and surjective onto the specified codomain Y; equivalently a function admitting a two-sided inverse Y→X. In structured settings this refers only to the underlying-set map, not to automatic continuity, R-linearity, group structure, or naturality.
items.mathematical_definition_draft: A function f:X→Y is bijective if it is injective and surjective onto Y. Equivalently, there exists a unique inverse function g:Y→X such that g∘f=id_X and f∘g=id_Y.
typed_assumptions_and_edge_cases: The unique empty function ∅→∅ is bijective.
A bijection of underlying sets is not automatically a homeomorphism, linear isomorphism or group isomorphism; structured morphism requirements are additional.
The specified codomain Y matters for surjectivity.

items.original_query: subfield k(B) generated by k and B
items.original_mathematical_context: Field theory: subfield k(B) of an extension K/k generated by k together with a subset B⊆K, the intersection of all intermediate subfields containing k∪B; for algebraically independent B, it identifies with a rational-function field in the elements of B.
items.term: Subfield generated by a subset over a base field
items.mathematical_definition_draft: Let K/k be a field extension and B⊆K. The subfield k(B) is the smallest intermediate subfield of K containing k and every element of B, equivalently the intersection of all subfields L with k∪B⊆L⊆K.
typed_assumptions_and_edge_cases: Elements of k(B) can be expressed as rational functions in finitely many members of B with coefficients in k and nonzero evaluated denominators.
If B is algebraically independent over k, k(B) is canonically isomorphic to a rational-function field indexed by B; without algebraic independence that identification may fail.

items.original_mathematical_context: Set theory: power set of an arbitrary underlying set X, namely the collection of all subsets of X; variable names X and S are interchangeable.
items.mathematical_definition_draft: For a set X, the power set P(X) (also written 𝒫(X)) is the set {A:A⊆X} of all subsets of X.
typed_assumptions_and_edge_cases: P(∅)={∅}, not the empty set.
∅∈P(X) and X∈P(X) for every set X.
This definition quantifies over a set X; a proper class generally has no set-valued power set under ZFC.

items.original_mathematical_context: Commutative algebra: square-zero ideal I of a commutative unital ring A, characterized by I²={0} (equivalently ab=0 for all a,b∈I). The square-zero property is strictly stronger than mere nilpotence of an unspecified positive exponent.
items.mathematical_definition_draft: An ideal I of a commutative ring R is square-zero if I²=(0). Equivalently, xy=0 for every x,y∈I.
typed_assumptions_and_edge_cases: The zero ideal is square-zero.
I²=(0) implies I is nilpotent, but an ideal with I³=0 need not have I²=0.
Each x∈I satisfies x²=0; the converse that every individual element squares to zero need not imply I²=0 in characteristic 2 (mixed products may survive).

items.original_mathematical_context: General topology: open neighborhood of a point x∈X, an open subset U of X containing x.
items.mathematical_definition_draft: Let (X,τ) be a topological space and x∈X. An open neighborhood of x is an open subset U∈τ such that x∈U.
typed_assumptions_and_edge_cases: Some sources call any set N containing an open neighborhood of x simply a neighborhood; this is broader than the open-neighborhood concept.
If X=∅, there are no points x for which the definition is instantiated.
For any point x, X itself is an open neighborhood.

items.original_mathematical_context: Commutative algebra: for unital ring homomorphism φ:R→S and prime q⊆S, contraction p=φ^{-1}(q)⊆R, a prime ideal by inverse-image stability under ring homomorphisms; when φ is an inclusion this becomes q∩R.
items.mathematical_definition_draft: Let φ:R→S be a unital homomorphism of commutative unital rings and q a prime ideal of S. The contraction of q to R is p=φ^{-1}(q)={r∈R:φ(r)∈q}; it is a prime ideal of R.
typed_assumptions_and_edge_cases: Properness uses φ(1_R)=1_S and 1_S∉q; without unitality the inverse image of a prime ideal need not be proper.
When φ is an inclusion R⊆S, the contraction is q∩R.
It is a structured instance of inverse image, not synonymous with that general set-theoretic operation.

items.original_mathematical_context: Elementary number theory: positive integer p greater than one whose positive divisors are exactly 1 and p; this is an integer prime, not a prime ideal of a ring.
items.mathematical_definition_draft: A positive integer p is prime if p>1 and its only positive divisors are 1 and p.
typed_assumptions_and_edge_cases: The integer 1 is not prime.
The number 2 is prime; no other even positive integer is prime.
This does not define a prime ideal, although (p) is prime in ℤ precisely when p is a prime integer (with the usual convention).

items.original_query: maximal element of a collection under inclusion
items.original_mathematical_context: Order theory: a maximal element m in a nonempty family F of subsets of an ambient set, ordered by inclusion, is one with no distinct member B∈F properly containing m. Maximal need not mean greatest, and for ideals the family F is any specified nonempty subcollection of the ideals of R.
items.mathematical_definition_draft: Let F be a family of subsets of a set X. An element M∈F is maximal with respect to inclusion if there is no B∈F satisfying M⊊B; equivalently, M⊆B for B∈F forces B=M.
typed_assumptions_and_edge_cases: A maximal member need not contain every other member; that would be a greatest element.
A nonempty family can fail to possess maximal members (for example finite subsets of ℕ ordered by inclusion).
The definition applies to a specified family of ideals as well as to other ordered families; do not assume every maximal ideal in a special family is a ring-theoretic maximal proper ideal.

items.original_mathematical_context: Category theory: parallel morphisms f,g:X→Y in a category, with identical source and codomain, forming a parallel-pair diagram.
items.mathematical_definition_draft: In a category C, two morphisms f,g are parallel if they have the same domain X and codomain Y, so f,g:X→Y.
typed_assumptions_and_edge_cases: Parallel does not require f and g to be distinct.
The diagram f,g:X⇉Y is a pair of arrows, not necessarily an equalizer, coequalizer, or other universal construction.
Hom_C(X,Y) is the ambient collection containing both arrows.

items.original_query: R-algebra isomorphism from the quotient to S
items.original_mathematical_context: Commutative algebra: isomorphism of unital R-algebras preserving both ring operations and the specified structure maps from R; not merely an abstract ring or R-module isomorphism.
items.mathematical_definition_draft: For unital R-algebras (A,ι_A),(B,ι_B), an R-algebra isomorphism is a bijective unital ring homomorphism f:A→B satisfying f∘ι_A=ι_B; equivalently, a ring isomorphism fixing the specified action of R.
typed_assumptions_and_edge_cases: The inverse of a bijective unital R-algebra homomorphism is an R-algebra homomorphism.
An underlying ring isomorphism need not preserve the specified R-algebra structures.
An R-linear module isomorphism need not preserve multiplication or identity.

items.original_mathematical_context: Commutative algebra: evaluation R-algebra homomorphism ev_(a_i):R[X_i : i∈I]→A into a commutative unital R-algebra A, sending each formal indeterminate X_i to a specified a_i∈A and fixing the coefficients through the structure map R→A; includes univariate evaluation f(a) and the canonical R[X_s:s∈S]→S sending X_s to s.
items.term: Evaluation homomorphism for a polynomial algebra
items.mathematical_definition_draft: Let R be a commutative unital ring, I a set, A a commutative unital R-algebra with structure ι:R→A, and (a_i)_{i∈I} a family of elements of A. The evaluation map ev_a:R[X_i:i∈I]→A is the unique R-algebra homomorphism with ev_a(X_i)=a_i for all i, and ev_a(r)=ι(r) on coefficients; it sends each polynomial to its finite coefficient-weighted sum of monomial evaluations.
typed_assumptions_and_edge_cases: Finite support of each polynomial makes evaluation well defined even if I is infinite.
Surjectivity requires that the elements a_i generate A as an R-algebra; it does not hold automatically.
For I=∅ this map is just the R-algebra structure homomorphism.

items.original_mathematical_context: Probability theory: finite absolute expectation E|X_t|<∞ of the real random variable X_t for every real time t≥0 in a stochastic process.
items.term: Integrability of a real random variable
items.mathematical_definition_draft: A real-valued measurable random variable X on a probability space (Ω,Σ,P) is integrable if E[|X|]=∫_Ω |X| dP is finite. For a process (X_t)_{t≥0}, requiring E[|X_t|]<∞ for every t≥0 means that each time marginal X_t is integrable.
typed_assumptions_and_edge_cases: Pointwise integrability for every fixed t does not imply sup_t E|X_t|<∞ or uniform integrability of the family.
An integrable X has a finite expectation E[X]; E[X] being undefined due to ∞−∞ is excluded by the absolute-integrability condition.
This does not assert stochastic-process path regularity or measurability jointly in t and ω.

items.original_mathematical_context: Commutative algebra/algebraic geometry: locus V(I)={p∈Spec(R):I⊆p} of prime ideals containing an ideal I in a commutative ring; these provide Zariski closed subsets.
items.term: Zariski-closed set determined by an ideal
items.mathematical_definition_draft: For a commutative ring R and ideal I⊆R, define V(I)={p∈Spec(R):I⊆p}, where Spec(R) is the set of prime ideals. The sets V(I) are exactly the closed sets of the Zariski topology on Spec(R).
typed_assumptions_and_edge_cases: V((0))=Spec(R), while V(R)=∅.
V(IJ)=V(I)∪V(J); these equalities are properties of the locus construction, not additional definition requirements.

items.original_mathematical_context: Topology: subset U⊆Spec(R) both Zariski-open and Zariski-closed, an instance of the generic clopen predicate, not the idempotent correspondence itself.
items.mathematical_definition_draft: Let (X,τ) be a topological space. A subset U⊆X is clopen if both U and X\U are open in X, equivalently if U is both open and closed.
typed_assumptions_and_edge_cases: ∅ and X are clopen in every topological space.
If X is connected, these are the only clopen subsets.
For X=Spec(R), clopen subsets correspond to suitable ring idempotents in commutative unital algebra; this theorem is not the definition of clopen.

items.original_query: closed subset of a topological space
items.original_mathematical_context: General topology: closed F⊆X exactly when X\F is open in the specified topology; this depends on the ambient X and is distinct from Zariski-closed subschemes.
items.term: Closed subset of a topological space
items.mathematical_definition_draft: Let (X,τ) be a topological space. A subset F⊆X is closed if its complement X\F is a member of τ, i.e. is open in X.
typed_assumptions_and_edge_cases: The empty set and X are always closed.
A subset may be both open and closed; closed does not mean 'not open'.
The definition depends on the ambient topology and is not equivalent to the extra structure of a closed subscheme.

items.original_query: roots of a polynomial in a field
items.original_mathematical_context: Polynomial algebra over fields: a root (zero) α∈K of a univariate polynomial f∈F[x] in a field extension K/F means f(α)=0_K using coefficient inclusion F→K and polynomial evaluation; includes the residue class of x in K=F[x]/(f) for nonconstant f.
items.term: Root of a polynomial over a field extension
items.mathematical_definition_draft: Let F⊆K be a field extension, f(T)=Σ_{j=0}^n a_j T^j∈F[T], and α∈K. The element α is a root (zero) of f in K if f(α)=Σ_j a_j α^j=0_K.
typed_assumptions_and_edge_cases: For the zero polynomial, every α∈K is a root; multiplicity conventions need a separate treatment.
The class x mod (f) is a root in the quotient F[x]/(f) for nonconstant f, but this quotient is a field only if f is irreducible; otherwise it is generally merely an F-algebra.
If f is nonconstant and irreducible, F[x]/(f) is a field and the residue class of x supplies a root in that field.
